questions.explanation:
Why This Is Asked
Tests ConfigMap usage, file-based config in a mounted volume, and in-app dynamic behavior without restarts. Checks readiness/liveness best practices and basic NetworkPolicy scoping.

Key Concepts
- ConfigMaps mounted as files
- Polling for dynamic config reload
- Readiness and liveness probes
- Namespace NetworkPolicy restricting egress

Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: flags-config
  namespace: default
data:
  flags.json: |
    {"enableFeature": true}
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: flag-tester
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: flag-tester
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: flag-tester
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: your-registry/flag-tester:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - name: flags
          mountPath: /etc/flags/flags.json
          subPath: flags.json
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
      - name: flags
        configMap:
          name: flags-config
```

Follow-up Questions
- How would you test config-change reload without pod restart?
- What limitations exist with polling vs. watching a ConfigMap mount?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests CKAD fundamentals for per-namespace automation, using CronJobs, ConfigMaps, Secrets, InitContainers, and PVC-backed logs in a realistic heartbeat scenario.

## Key Concepts

- CronJob scheduling and Job templates
- ConfigMap and Secret usage for config and creds
- InitContainer for one-time setup
- Probes for container health
- PersistentVolumeClaim for logs

## Code Example

```javascript
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: heartbeat-cron
  namespace: default
spec:
  schedule: "*/10 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
          - name: install-deps
            image: alpine:3.19
            command: ["sh","-c","apk add --no-cache curl"]
          containers:
          - name: heartbeater
            image: alpine:3.19
            command: ["sh","-c","curl -sS -X POST -H \"Authorization: Bearer $API_TOKEN\" $TARGET_URL/heartbeat -d '{\"ts\": \"$(date +%s)\"}'"]
            envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: cron-config
            - secretRef:
                name: target-creds
            volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
            readinessProbe:
              exec:
                command: ["sh","-c","test -f /logs/ready"]
              initialDelaySeconds: 5
              periodSeconds: 10
            livenessProbe:
              httpGet:
                path: /healthz
                port: 80
              initialDelaySeconds: 15
              periodSeconds: 20
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          volumes:
          - name: logs
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: heartbeat-logs
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you rotate the API token without recreating the CronJob?
- What failure modes and retries would you implement?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to compose common CKAD primitives into a cohesive, maintainable per-namespace app: InitContainer logic, ConfigMap-driven behavior, TLS handling, and network isolation.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainer installs rendering tool and pre-processes inputs
- ConfigMap and Secret drive runtime config and secrets
- Sidecar for TLS rotation and secret refresh
- Readiness/Liveness probes for quick failure detection
- Namespace NetworkPolicy restricts egress to internal endpoints

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: docs-portal
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: docs-portal
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: docs-portal
    spec:
      volumes:
        - name: docs
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: docs-pvc
        - name: tls-cert
          secret:
            secretName: docs-tls
      initContainers:
        - name: render-md
          image: pandoc/pandoc:latest
          command: ["sh", "-c", "cp -r /docs/* /rendered/; pandoc -f markdown -t html /docs/*.md -o /rendered/index.html"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: docs
              mountPath: /docs
            - name: rendered
              mountPath: /rendered
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:stable
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
          volumeMounts:
            - name: rendered
              mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 80
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 80
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 20
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle new Markdown files added at runtime?
- How would you scale this per-namespace deployment with multiple replicas?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
CKAD requires practical mastery of node-scoped components, DaemonSets, hostPath volumes, and real-world log shipping patterns.

## Key Concepts
- DaemonSet on each node with hostPath volumes
- Log tailing with tail -F and sidecar shipping
- ConfigMap-driven batching (BATCH_SIZE)
- NodeSelector to target workers
- Readiness/Liveness probes and lifecycle (preStop)
- Resource requests/limits and rollback strategy

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: log-collector
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: log-collector
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: log-collector
    spec:
      nodeSelector:
        kubernetes.io/os: linux
      containers:
      - name: collector
        image: busybox:stable
        command: ["sh","-c","tail -F /var/log/app.log | /usr/local/bin/shipper --endpoint http://log-portal:5000/api/v1/logs --batch-size $(BUS_BATCH)" ]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /var/log
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "256Mi"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 15
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /ready
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 30
        lifecycle:
          preStop:
            exec:
              command: ["sh","-c","sleep 10"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /var/log
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        hostPath:
          path: /var/log
          type: Directory
``` 

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test under burst log loads and verify end-to-end delivery? 
- How would you rollback a DaemonSet rollout if a regression is found?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Explores practical CKAD competencies: deployment orchestration, config/secret management, volumes, autoscaling, service exposure, and network isolation.

## Key Concepts
- Deployment, PVC, ConfigMap/Secret, HPA
- ClusterIP service semantics
- NetworkPolicy gating and its limitations

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-app
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: my-app:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: my-app-config
        - secretRef:
            name: my-app-creds
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
      volumes:
      - name: data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: data-pvc
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: data-pvc
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
  storageClassName: standard
---
apiVersion: autoscaling/v1
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: my-app-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: my-app
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 10
  targetCPUUtilizationPercentage: 60
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-app
spec:
  selector:
    app: my-app
  ports:
  - port: 8080
    targetPort: 8080
  type: ClusterIP
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-egress-api
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-app
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 203.0.113.0/24
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 443
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test this in a cluster with a restricted CNI?
- What changes if the app becomes stateful or requires dynamic PVC provisioning?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests CKAD ability to combine common primitives: PVC-backed data, ConfigMap-driven behavior, Secrets for credentials, InitContainers, TLS rotation sidecar, probes, and per-namespace NetworkPolicy in a cohesive, beginner-friendly scenario.

## Key Concepts
- ConfigMap/Secret usage for runtime config and credentials
- PVC-backed storage and data lifecycle
- InitContainer for dependencies
- TLS cert rotation sidecar
- Readiness/Liveness probes and health checks
- NamespaceNetworkPolicy scoping

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: ns-api
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: ns-api
    spec:
      volumes:
        - name: data
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: ns-app-data
      initContainers:
        - name: install-deps
          image: python:3.11
          command: ["bash","-lc","pip install flask sqlite3"]
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: myregistry/ns-api:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          env:
            - name: ENABLE_FEATURE
              valueFrom:
                configMapKeyRef:
                  name: app-config
                  key: ENABLE_FEATURE
            - name: API_TIMEOUT
              valueFrom:
                configMapKeyRef:
                  name: app-config
                  key: API_TIMEOUT
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data
      - name: tls-sidecar
        image: quay.io/cert_manager/tls-sidecar:latest
        # sidecar config omitted for brevity
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      restartPolicy: Always
```

## Follow-up Questions

questions.explanation:
## Why This Matters
This question tests critical CKAD competencies: initializing pods with InitContainers, configuring volume mounts for data sharing, implementing zero-downtime deployments, and ensuring availability during disruptions with PodDisruptionBudgets.

## Key Concepts

- **InitContainer**: Runs to completion before main containers start. Uses the same volume mounts to share data with the main container. Multiple init containers run sequentially.

- **Volume Mounts**: The ConfigMap is mounted at `/config` for the init container to access `cache-base`. An `emptyDir` volume shares `/var/cache` between init and main containers.

- **RollingUpdate maxUnavailable: 0**: Critical for zero-downtime updates. Ensures all 3 pods update one at a time, with a new pod fully ready before the old one terminates.

- **PodDisruptionBudget minAvailable: 2**: With 3 replicas, guarantees at least 2 pods remain healthy during voluntary disruptions (node drains, API server issues). This prevents service degradation.

## Common Pitfalls

1. **Missing volumeMounts in init container** - InitContainer cannot access volumes without explicit mountPath
2. **maxUnavailable set to 1** - Can cause brief unavailability during rolling updates
3. **PDB selector mismatch** - Must match the Deployment's pod selector exactly
4. **Forgetting emptyDir for /var/cache** - Without a volume, /var/cache would be lost on container restart

        spec:

## Why This Is Asked

Tests CKAD fundamentals in a realistic nightly QA workflow: CronJobs, per-namespace isolation, PVC usage, ConfigMap/Secret mounts, InitContainer dependency management, TLS rotation sidecar, health probes, and restrictive NetworkPolicy. Also evaluates data validation patterns and architectural trade-offs.

## Key Concepts

- CronJob scheduling and namespace isolation
- PVC data persistence and volume mounting
- ConfigMap/Secret mounting and environment injection
- InitContainer for runtime dependency installation
- Sidecar pattern for TLS certificate rotation
- Readiness/Liveness probe implementation
- NetworkPolicy egress restrictions
- Python data validation with pandas/jsonschema

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: data-qa-cronjob
  namespace: example
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
          - name: install-deps
            image: python:3.9-alpine
            command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - |
              pip install pandas==1.3.3 jsonschema==3.2.0 --target /app/deps
            volumeMounts:
            - name: deps-volume
              mountPath: /app/deps
          containers:
          - name: validator
            image: python:3.9-alpine
            command:
            - python
            - -c
            - |
              import sys
              sys.path.append('/app/deps')
              import os
              import pandas as pd
              import jsonschema
              import requests
              from datetime import datetime
              
              schema_path = os.getenv('SCHEMA_PATH', '/data/schema.json')
              date_range = os.getenv('DATE_RANGE', '7')
              
              # Load schema
              with open(schema_path) as f:
                  schema = json.load(f)
              
              # Validate CSVs
              for csv_file in os.listdir('/data'):
                  if csv_file.endswith('.csv'):
                      df = pd.read_csv(f'/data/{csv_file}')
                      try:
                          jsonschema.validate(df.to_dict('records'), schema)
                          result = {'file': csv_file, 'status': 'pass', 'timestamp': datetime.utcnow().isoformat()}
                      except Exception as e:
                          result = {'file': csv_file, 'status': 'fail', 'error': str(e), 'timestamp': datetime.utcnow().isoformat()}
                      
                      # Send to QA portal
                      requests.post('http://qa-portal:8090/api/v1/qa', 
                                   json=result,
                                   headers={'Authorization': f"Bearer {os.getenv('QA_TOKEN')}"})
            envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: app-config
            - secretRef:
                name: qa-credentials
            volumeMounts:
            - name: data-volume
              mountPath: /data
            - name: deps-volume
              mountPath: /app/deps
              readOnly: true
            readinessProbe:
              exec:
                command:
                - python
                - -c
                - "import pandas, jsonschema, requests"
              initialDelaySeconds: 10
              periodSeconds: 5
            livenessProbe:
              exec:
                command:
                - python
                - -c
                - "import sys; sys.exit(0)"
              initialDelaySeconds: 30
              periodSeconds: 30
          - name: cert-rotator
            image: cert-manager/cert-manager-rotator:v1.8.0
            args:
            - --watch-cert-dir=/certs
            - --cert-secret-name=qa-tls-cert
            volumeMounts:
            - name: cert-volume
              mountPath: /certs
          volumes:
          - name: data-volume
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: data-pvc
          - name: deps-volume
            emptyDir: {}
          - name: cert-volume
            emptyDir: {}
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
  namespace: example
data:
  SCHEMA_PATH: "/data/schema.json"
  DATE_RANGE: "7"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: qa-credentials
  namespace: example
type: Opaque
data:
  QA_TOKEN: <base64-encoded-token>
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: qa-egress-policy
  namespace: example
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      job-name: data-qa-cronjob
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: qa-namespace
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8090
```

## Trade-offs

**CronJob vs Deployment**: CronJob provides scheduled execution but lacks continuous monitoring. A Deployment could run continuously but would require external coordination.

**InitContainer Pattern**: Ensures dependencies are available but increases startup time and complexity. Using a pre-built image would be faster but reduces flexibility.

**Sidecar for TLS**: Separates concerns and enables independent updates but adds resource overhead and coordination complexity.

**NetworkPolicy Restriction**: Enhances security but requires careful rule management and monitoring to avoid blocking legitimate traffic.

**PVC for Data**: Ensures persistence across runs but creates coupling between namespaces and requires careful capacity planning.

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question assesses familiarity with ConfigMap mounts, InitContainers, and sidecar reload patterns within a single namespace. It also evaluates understanding of signal-based versus in-process reload mechanisms, along with basic security practices using Secrets and NetworkPolicies.

## Key Concepts
- **ConfigMap-driven runtime config**: Externalizing configuration allows updates without rebuilding containers
- **InitContainer provisioning**: Installing tooling (inotify-tools) needed by sidecars or main containers
- **Sidecar watching**: File change detection using inotifywait triggers graceful reloads without container restart
- **Signal-based reloads**: SIGHUP triggers graceful reloads; alternative approaches include local /reload API endpoints
- **Security with Secrets**: Sensitive data like admin credentials should mount via Secrets, not environment variables
- **NetworkPolicy**: Namespace-level egress restrictions limit exposure of internal endpoints

## Trade-offs
- **Signal vs. API reload**: SIGHUP requires the application to handle signals gracefully; /reload APIs add complexity but offer finer control
- **inotifywait vs. polling**: inotifywait is event-driven and efficient but limited to the container filesystem; polling works cross-platform but incurs overhead
- **Sidecar vs. embedded reload**: Sidecars keep concerns separated but add resource overhead; embedding reload logic reduces complexity but couples concerns
- **ConfigMap vs. volume plugins**: Native ConfigMap mounts require pod recreation for updates; external volume plugins enable dynamic updates at the cost of complexity

## Why This Is Asked

Tests CRD API access from a pod, ConfigMap-driven runtime configuration, Secret-based credentials, InitContainer usage, and proper observability with probes and PVC-backed logs. It also touches network isolation via NetworkPolicy in a CKAD-appropriate setting.

## Key Concepts

- CRD watch and API access from a namespace-scoped Pod
- ConfigMap as dynamic WINDOW configuration
- Secret-stored Bearer token for outbound POST
- InitContainer for tooling installation
- Readiness/Liveness probes for a long-running auditor
- Logs persisted to a PVC
- Namespace NetworkPolicy restricting egress

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
data:
  audit-config: |
    window: 60
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
data:
  audit-token: <base64-encoded-token>
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: crd-auditor
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: crd-auditor
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: crd-auditor
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: crd-auditor-sa
      initContainers:
      - name: install-tools
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl jq"]
        volumeMounts:
        - mountPath: /logs
          name: logs
      containers:
      - name: auditor
        image: my-registry/crd-auditor:latest
        env:
        - name: AUDIT_CONFIG
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: audit-config
              key: window
        - name: AUDIT_TOKEN
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: audit-token
              key: token
        volumeMounts:
        - mountPath: /logs
          name: logs
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: crd-auditor-logs
```

- How would you handle CRD API version upgrades and backward compatibility?

Why This Is Asked
Tests per-namespace operational hardening: config-driven behavior, rolling restarts, health checks, lifecycle hooks, and disruption budgets in CKAD context.

Key Concepts
- ConfigMap-driven behavior with pod template checksum for rolling restarts
- Tail/log ingestion from a PVC-backed path
- Probes: readiness /healthz, liveness /livez
- Resource requests/limits and lifecycle preStop
- PodDisruptionBudget to guarantee minimum healthy pods

Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: log-processor
  namespace: audit
spec:
  replicas: 4
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        checksum/config: "<checksum-from-configmap>"
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: processor
        image: myrepo/log-processor:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /var/log/stream
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "200m"
            memory: "256Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "512Mi"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /livez
            port: 8080
        lifecycle:
          preStop:
            exec:
              command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 10"]
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: log-stream-pvc
```

- How would you simulate load and verify throughput vs. reliability?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design a safe, observable canary rollout using standard Kubernetes resources and NGINX Ingress without a service mesh.

## Key Concepts
- Canary deployment pattern with separate Deployments
- Ingress annotations (nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary, canary-weight)
- Progressive traffic shifting and rollback strategy
- Observability: latency, error rate, saturation

## Code Example
```yaml
# Stable Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: frontend
  namespace: prod
  labels:
    app: frontend
    version: stable
spec:
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: frontend
      version: stable
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: frontend
        version: stable
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: frontend
        image: frontend:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
```
```yaml
# Canary Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: frontend-canary
  namespace: prod
  labels:
    app: frontend
    version: canary
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: frontend
      version: canary
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: frontend
        version: canary
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: frontend
        image: frontend:1.2-canary
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
```
```yaml
# Ingress (production path)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: frontend-ingress
  namespace: prod
  annotations:
    # enable canary routing for the canary backend
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-weight: "10"
spec:
  rules:
  - host: "frontend.example.com"
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: frontend-canary
            port:
              number: 80
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you promote canary to 50% and then 100% safely?
- What metrics would you monitor to decide progression or rollback?
- How would you rollback if the canary fails without affecting stable users?
